overview.headline: How legislative, judicial, and executive branches share power

keyPoints.point: The Constitution divides the federal government into legislative, judicial, and executive branches
keyPoints.quote: The Constitution of the United States divides the federal government into three branches:

keyPoints.point: Legislative branch handles confirming or rejecting presidential nominations for federal agencies and judges
keyPoints.quote: Confirming or rejecting presidential nominations for heads of federal agencies, federal judges, and the Supreme Court

keyPoints.point: Judicial branch focuses on deciding if laws violate the Constitution
keyPoints.quote: Deciding if laws violate the Constitution

keyPoints.point: Each branch can respond to actions of other branches through the system of checks and balances
keyPoints.quote: The ability of each branch to respond to the actions of the other branches is the system of checks and balances.

keyTerms.gloss: elected Congress group focused on legislative lawmaking duties
keyTerms.quote: The legislative branch is made up of Congress:

keyTerms.gloss: court system focused on judicial review of laws
keyTerms.quote: The judicial branch includes the Supreme Court and other federal courts.

keyTerms.gloss: presidential leadership group directing executive actions
keyTerms.quote: The president, the vice president, and the president's cabinet are the members of the executive branch.

keyTerms.gloss: system where branches check each others actions
keyTerms.quote: The ability of each branch to respond to the actions of the other branches is the system of checks and balances.

keyTerms.gloss: advisors nominated to guide cabinet departments
keyTerms.quote: The cabinet members serve as advisors to the president.
